questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a trading bloc?
options: A group of countries that have agreed to reduce or remove trade barriers between themselves
A group of businesses that agree to fix prices
An international body that settles trade disputes
A group of countries sharing a single currency only
questions.why: Blocs range from a free trade area up to a monetary union.
whyNot: That is a cartel.
That is the WTO.
A monetary union is one particular level of integration.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a customs union from a free trade area?
options: A customs union applies a common external tariff to non-members
A customs union allows free movement of labour
A customs union uses a single currency
A free trade area has no internal tariffs, while a customs union does
questions.why: The common external tariff also removes the rules-of-origin problem and removes members' freedom to set their own trade policy.
whyNot: Free movement of labour comes with a single market.
A single currency comes with a monetary union.
Both remove internal tariffs.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a single market?
options: A customs union that also allows free movement of goods, services, capital and labour
A market in which only one product is traded
A market with a single dominant supplier
A free trade area with a shared currency
questions.why: Harmonised standards mean a product approved in one member is accepted in all.
whyNot: The term refers to integration between countries, not to one product.
That is a monopoly.
A shared currency is a monetary union, and a single market need not have one.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines trade creation?
options: The increase in trade between bloc members that results from removing barriers between them
The shift of trade away from an efficient non-member to a less efficient member
The creation of new products for export
The establishment of a new trading bloc
questions.why: Creation is the genuine gain from a bloc; diversion is the loss.
whyNot: That is trade diversion.
That is product development.
That is the formation of a bloc, not trade creation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines trade diversion?
options: Trade shifting from a more efficient non-member to a less efficient member because of the external tariff
Trade shifting from goods to services
Trade being redirected through a third country to avoid duty
Trade falling because of a recession
questions.why: Whether a bloc is beneficial overall depends on whether creation or diversion is larger.
whyNot: That is structural change in trade composition.
That is transhipment or duty avoidance.
That is a cyclical fall in trade.

questions.stem: Why are rules of origin needed in a free trade area?
options: To stop goods entering through the member with the lowest external tariff
To identify which member produced the most exports
To decide which currency a transaction is priced in
To ensure products meet safety standards
questions.why: Because each member keeps its own external tariffs, goods could otherwise enter cheaply and circulate freely. A customs union removes the problem.
whyNot: The rules concern the origin of goods, not export league tables.
Pricing currency is unrelated.
Safety is covered by product standards.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit for a business inside a trading bloc?
options: A larger tariff-free market and therefore greater economies of scale
Protection from competitors based in other member states
Freedom from all product regulation
A guarantee of higher prices
questions.why: Production can also be concentrated where it is most efficient and shipped throughout the bloc.
whyNot: Removing barriers exposes the business to those competitors.
Bloc-wide regulation may be stricter than the national rules it replaced.
More competition typically pushes prices down.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cost for a business inside a trading bloc?
options: More competition from other members' firms in its home market
Higher tariffs on sales to other members
The loss of access to its own domestic market
A requirement to adopt a new currency immediately
questions.why: The removal of barriers works in both directions, which is the point students most often omit.
whyNot: Internal tariffs are removed, not raised.
Domestic access is unaffected.
Only a monetary union involves a shared currency.

questions.stem: Which bloc named in the specification is a single market with a monetary union among most members?
options: The EU
ASEAN
NAFTA
The WTO
questions.why: The EU is the deepest integration of the three named, with harmonised standards and common competition rules.
whyNot: ASEAN is looser, closer to a free trade area with cooperation.
NAFTA was a free trade area, replaced in 2020 by the USMCA.
The WTO is not a trading bloc.

questions.stem: Why were rules of origin central to NAFTA?
options: It was a free trade area, so a stated proportion of value had to originate within the bloc to qualify
It was a monetary union with a shared currency
It applied a common external tariff
It allowed free movement of labour between members
questions.why: That requirement drove manufacturers to source and assemble within North America, reshaping supply chains rather than simply cutting prices.
whyNot: There was no shared currency.
A common external tariff would have made it a customs union.
Free movement of labour was not part of the agreement.

questions.stem: Why do trading blocs attract FDI from non-members?
options: A product made inside the bloc circulates tariff-free, while an import faces the common external tariff
Blocs offer lower corporation tax to all foreign investors
Non-members are legally required to invest inside blocs
Production costs inside blocs are always lower
questions.why: This is a benefit to the bloc and a cost to the business, which has to make a large investment it would otherwise avoid.
whyNot: Tax rates are set by individual members, not by the bloc.
No such requirement exists.
Costs inside may be higher; the tariff is what tips the decision.

questions.stem: What does a member give up by joining a monetary union?
options: The ability to set its own interest rate or let its currency adjust
The ability to trade with non-members
Control over its own tax rates
The right to leave the union
questions.why: That loss matters when a member needs a different monetary stance from the rest of the union.
whyNot: Trade with non-members continues, subject to the external tariff.
Taxation generally remains a national matter.
Membership is not irrevocable.

questions.stem: How should a business outside a bloc respond to the common external tariff?
options: Weigh exporting and absorbing the tariff against investing inside the bloc or licensing a local producer
Immediately withdraw from the market entirely
Lobby the WTO to abolish the bloc
Ignore the tariff, since it is paid by the customer
questions.why: The choice depends on the size of the tariff, the expected volume and how permanent the bloc's arrangements look.
whyNot: Withdrawal is one option among several and rarely the first.
The WTO permits regional agreements.
The duty is paid on import and affects the delivered price and the business's competitiveness.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a common external tariff?
options: A single tariff applied by all members of a customs union to imports from outside the bloc
The average of members' individual tariffs on each other
A tariff charged on trade between members
A tariff set by the WTO for all countries
questions.why: It is what distinguishes a customs union from a free trade area.
whyNot: It is a single agreed rate, not an average.
Internal trade between members is tariff-free.
The WTO does not set tariff rates.

questions.stem: Why is the trade-off of bloc membership sharper for a very small economy?
options: There is little domestic industry to protect and a great deal of market to gain
Small economies are never admitted to blocs
Small economies must adopt the shared currency immediately
Small economies face higher external tariffs than large ones
questions.why: Membership provides access to a market far larger than its own while reducing its ability to protect what little domestic industry it has.
whyNot: Small economies are members of many blocs.
Currency adoption applies only to monetary unions.
The external tariff is common to all members.

questions.stem: A bloc's external tariff forces a business to buy from a less efficient member instead of a cheaper non-member. What is this?
options: Trade diversion, which raises the business's costs
Trade creation, which lowers the business's costs
Economies of scale
Regulatory arbitrage
questions.why: Diversion shifts trade to the wrong producer, and it is the main economic criticism of blocs.
whyNot: Creation means more trade with efficient producers.
Scale economies concern volume and unit cost.
That means locating activity where rules are weakest.
